inputs.need:
I am a pediatric hospitalist at a 180-bed children's hospital. Every winter our general pediatric ward cares for 250 to 300 infants with bronchiolitis, and about 40 percent of them are started on high-flow nasal cannula in the emergency department or on the ward. Starting high flow follows a protocol, but stopping it does not: each attending weans differently. Some step the flow down by 1 litre per kilogram every few hours, others stop it outright once the infant looks comfortable in low oxygen. Our median time on high flow last winter was 52 hours, and families often ask why their baby is still on it when they look well.

A group of us drafted a weaning protocol: once an infant has been stable for two hours on FiO2 of 40 percent or less, high flow is stopped directly with a trial off instead of stepping down, with defined criteria for restarting. Some of our PICU colleagues worry that direct cessation leads to more re-escalation, particularly in younger infants, and the papers they sent us seem to disagree.

I am not sure how to evaluate this. We could run it as a quality improvement project with PDSA cycles over the coming winter, or we could do a before-after cohort comparison of this winter's infants against last winter's using the charts. The outcomes we care about are time on high flow, length of stay, and safety: restarting high flow, PICU transfer, and readmission within 7 days. Nurses and respiratory therapists would do the two-hourly checks, and nights are short-staffed. We have no research funding, and the season starts in about six weeks.
inputs.constraints: No research funding. The weaning protocol has to start with the winter season in November 2026. Two-hourly checks must fit existing nurse and respiratory therapist staffing, which is thinner at night. Evaluation data must come from the chart plus a short bedside log.
localFacts: The pediatric department's quality committee screened the weaning protocol as quality improvement on 2026-09-15 (screening QC-PED-2026-044).
The PICU and ward medical leads signed off the draft weaning protocol, version 1.2, on 2026-09-18.
From November 2025 to March 2026, 276 infants with bronchiolitis were admitted to the ward; 112 received high flow, with a median of 52 hours on high flow.
Respiratory therapists cover the ward from 07:00 to 23:00; overnight respiratory checks are done by nurses.

response.title: Direct-cessation weaning of high-flow nasal cannula for infants with bronchiolitis on a general pediatric ward
response.subtitle: Evaluation design not yet settled: improvement cycles or a before-after comparison
response.statement: Infants with bronchiolitis spend a median of 52 hours on high-flow nasal cannula on the general pediatric ward, partly because weaning varies between attendings. A drafted protocol stops high flow directly after two stable hours in FiO2 of 40 percent or less. The team needs to know whether the protocol shortens time on high flow and length of stay without more re-escalation, PICU transfer or readmission, particularly in young infants, and how to evaluate it within one season.
response.whoAffected: Infants with bronchiolitis on high flow (about 110 a season), their parents, ward nurses and respiratory therapists who do the checks, and the PICU team that receives infants who deteriorate.
response.whatHurts: Unnecessary hours on high flow delay feeding, holding and discharge, and inconsistent weaning confuses families; stopping too early in a vulnerable infant could lead to re-escalation or PICU transfer.
response.currentPractice: Weaning is at each attending's discretion, stepwise or direct, with no shared criteria for a trial off or for restarting.
response.whyNow: The protocol has been drafted and signed off, the season starts in November, and families keep asking why weaning takes so long.
response.constraints: No research funding. The weaning protocol has to start with the winter season in November 2026. Two-hourly checks must fit existing nurse and respiratory therapist staffing, which is thinner at night. Evaluation data must come from the chart plus a short bedside log.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Infants come off high flow as soon as it is safe, go home sooner and are not harmed by stopping too early, and parents know the criteria for stopping and restarting.
response.summary: Problem framed; the evaluation design is left unresolved between improvement cycles and a before-after comparison until the evidence has been reviewed.

records.title: Direct cessation versus stepwise weaning of high-flow nasal cannula in infants with bronchiolitis: a randomised trial
records.authors: Okonjo-Reyes A, Lindqvist-Barros M, Tamura-Holt E
records.abstract: We randomly allocated 184 infants aged 1 to 24 months with bronchiolitis on high-flow nasal cannula to direct cessation once stable for two hours in FiO2 of 40 percent or less, or to stepwise weaning of flow. Time on high flow was shorter with direct cessation (median 26 against 44 hours), and length of stay fell by a median of 18 hours. Re-escalation to high flow within 24 hours occurred in 11 percent with direct cessation and 8 percent with stepwise weaning, a difference compatible with chance. Infants younger than 3 months made up 21 percent of participants. No infant required intubation.

records.title: Re-escalation after abrupt discontinuation of high-flow support in young infants: a multicentre observational study
records.abstract: Across five pediatric wards, we compared 1,030 infants with bronchiolitis whose high flow was stopped abruptly with those weaned stepwise, according to local practice. Among infants younger than 8 weeks, re-escalation within 48 hours occurred in 24 percent after abrupt discontinuation and 12 percent after stepwise weaning (adjusted odds ratio 2.1). In older infants there was no difference. PICU transfer was rare in both groups. Wards that used abrupt discontinuation also admitted younger and sicker infants, and residual confounding is likely.

records.title: A ward-based weaning protocol for high-flow nasal cannula in bronchiolitis: a quality improvement report
records.authors: Fitzsimmons-Obi K, Arakawa-Lund P, Mensah-Carlyle J
records.venue: Hospital Quality and Safety in Children
records.abstract: We introduced a nurse-driven weaning protocol for high-flow nasal cannula on a general pediatric ward over three PDSA cycles in one winter. Median time on high flow fell from 49 to 30 hours on the run chart, with a shift sustained for 11 weeks. Length of stay fell from 3.4 to 2.7 days. Readmission within 7 days was unchanged at 3 percent, and PICU transfers fell slightly. Protocol adherence at night was 62 percent compared with 85 percent during the day, and most missed trials off occurred after midnight.

records.title: Stepwise weaning is not needed after high-flow therapy in bronchiolitis: an individual patient analysis from three hospitals
records.abstract: Using routinely collected data from three hospitals, we analysed 2,410 episodes of high-flow therapy for bronchiolitis in infants under 12 months, comparing direct cessation with stepwise weaning. After adjustment for age, oxygen requirement and hospital, re-escalation within 24 hours did not differ (8.9 against 9.4 percent), including in infants younger than 8 weeks (13.1 against 12.4 percent). Time on high flow was 20 hours shorter with direct cessation. This preprint has not been peer reviewed, and its listing does not give a year of posting.

records.title: Parents' experience of high-flow nasal cannula and weaning decisions for infants with bronchiolitis
records.abstract: We held structured conversations with 32 parents of infants treated with high-flow nasal cannula on two pediatric wards. Parents described the high flow as frightening at first and later as a barrier to feeding and holding their baby. Many did not understand why weaning took so long once their baby looked well, and inconsistent explanations from different doctors increased their worry. Parents wanted to be told the criteria for stopping and restarting high flow. Conversations took place on the ward, which may have limited criticism.

records.title: Two-hourly respiratory assessments at night on pediatric wards: nurse workload during the bronchiolitis season
records.abstract: We timed respiratory assessments on three pediatric wards during a bronchiolitis season. A structured assessment took a median of 6 minutes, and nurses caring for four infants on high flow spent about a quarter of each night hour on assessments. Scheduled assessments were missed in 18 percent of night hours and 6 percent of day hours. Missed assessments were most common between 02:00 and 05:00. Wards with a respiratory therapist overnight missed fewer assessments. The authors suggest weaning protocols set assessment frequencies that night staffing can deliver.

records.title: Variation in high-flow weaning practice among pediatric hospitalists: a national survey
records.abstract: We surveyed 412 pediatric hospitalists about how they wean high-flow nasal cannula in bronchiolitis. Forty-six percent used stepwise flow reduction, 31 percent stopped high flow directly once oxygen requirements were low, and 23 percent varied by patient. Only 18 percent of respondents worked in hospitals with a written weaning protocol. Respondents who feared re-escalation most often cited young infant age and night-time staffing. Most respondents said they would follow a local protocol if one existed. The response rate was 44 percent, and hospitalists in teaching hospitals were over-represented.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A trial and a ward improvement report agree that direct cessation after a short stable period shortens time on high flow by roughly 18 to 20 hours without a clear rise in re-escalation. For infants younger than 8 weeks the evidence conflicts: a confounded observational study found re-escalation doubled after abrupt discontinuation, while an undated preprint found no difference; neither settles the question. Night assessments are often missed, and parents want clear criteria. The evidence supports testing the protocol locally for infants aged 8 weeks or older with close safety monitoring.
response.gradeRationale: One small trial with few young infants, one improvement report and conflicting observational evidence for the youngest infants; low certainty overall, very uncertain for infants under 8 weeks.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five claims recorded, one of them with high uncertainty because the evidence conflicts.

response.reading: Time on high flow is driven less by the infant than by the weaning habit of the attending on duty. Retrieved evidence supports direct cessation for most infants, but the question that worries the PICU team, safety in infants under 8 weeks, is exactly where the evidence conflicts (claim c3). The night is the weak link: checks are done by nurses alone and are often missed elsewhere (claim c4), which could both delay trials off and delay spotting re-escalation.

includes: Direct-cessation weaning of high-flow nasal cannula for infants with bronchiolitis on a general pediatric ward

response.rationale: The aim is to improve weaning on one ward within one season while adapting the protocol, especially its night-time delivery. Improvement cycles with weekly run charts suit this: the change is supported for infants aged 8 weeks or older (c1, c2), night delivery needs adapting between cycles (c4), and safety is watched with balancing measures. A before-after cohort comparison of two winters was considered and refused because season severity and staffing differ between years and a fixed protocol could not be adapted. The conflicting evidence on younger infants (c3) is handled by keeping stepwise weaning for them. Reporting follows SQUIRE 2.0.
alternatives: Before-after cohort comparison of the 2025 to 2026 and 2026 to 2027 seasons (refused: season severity and staffing confound it, and the protocol could not be adapted)
Direct cessation for all ages (refused: unresolved safety evidence under 8 weeks, claim c3)
Leave weaning to individual attendings (the status quo that produces 52-hour medians)
response.whyNotMoreComplex: A multi-site trial would be needed to settle the young-infant question; this ward's question is local improvement, which run charts and balancing measures can answer in one season.

decision.statement: Introduce the direct-cessation weaning protocol for infants aged 8 weeks or older in PDSA cycles from November 2026 to March 2027, keeping stepwise weaning for younger infants, with a weekly run chart of time on high flow and re-escalation, PICU transfer and 7-day readmission as balancing measures.

response.overview: Ward-level QI project over the 2026 to 2027 bronchiolitis season: weekly baseline points from the previous season's charts, then three PDSA cycles introducing and refining a direct-cessation weaning protocol for infants aged 8 weeks or older.
response.population: Infants aged 8 weeks or older with bronchiolitis on high-flow nasal cannula on the general pediatric ward; infants under 8 weeks continue stepwise weaning and are followed descriptively.
response.exposure: Once stable for two hours in FiO2 of 40 percent or less, high flow is stopped with a trial off; restart criteria are fixed in protocol version 1.2. A plain-language criteria card is given to parents.
response.procedures: Cycle 1 (November): day shifts only. Cycle 2 (December to January): 24 hours, with a fixed 22:00 assessment added if night trials off lag. Cycle 3 (February to March): refinements from cycle reviews. A bedside log records trial-off time, restarts and missed checks; the weekly run chart is reviewed at the ward huddle; the PICU lead reviews every re-escalation.

response.designSummary: Weekly run charts of time on high flow with pre-specified rules, plus p-charts and a stopping rule for safety balancing measures.
response.sampleSize: About 5 to 8 infants aged 8 weeks or older start high flow each week in season, about 90 over 20 weeks. Weekly medians from so few infants are noisy, so the chart uses two-week medians when a week has fewer than four infants. A fall from about 52 to 32 hours would give a shift of six or more points below the baseline median within the second cycle. For safety, 90 trials off give a 95 percent upper limit of about 18 percent if 10 percent re-escalate; the stopping rule (more than 15 percent over any four weeks, at least 12 trials off) is reviewed by the PICU lead rather than tested.
response.primaryAnalysis: Run chart of median hours on high flow with the baseline season's median as centre line and shift, trend and runs rules fixed in advance.
response.secondaryAnalysis: p-chart of re-escalation; counts of PICU transfers and 7-day readmissions; run chart of length of stay; adherence by day and night; descriptive outcomes for infants under 8 weeks on stepwise weaning.
response.missingData: Infants with missing stop times are traced in the chart by the ward clerk; any still missing are reported, not imputed.
response.multiplicity: One outcome measure carries the aim; balancing measures drive the stopping rule, not significance tests.
response.software: Spreadsheet run chart template kept by the ward's QI nurse and checked by the hospitalist lead.
overfittingGuards: Run chart and stopping rules fixed before November
Two-week medians used whenever a week has fewer than four infants
No subgroup testing beyond the age groups fixed by the protocol
response.summary: About 90 infants over the season; run chart rules for the aim and a pre-specified safety stopping rule.

response.risks: The protocol changes the timing of a routine step; the main risk is re-escalation or deterioration after stopping, mitigated by the age limit, restart criteria, PICU review of every re-escalation and a stopping rule.
response.consent: Screened as quality improvement; parents receive the criteria card and are told the ward is using a new weaning protocol; they can ask for stepwise weaning and the attending may decline a trial off for clinical reasons.
response.data: The bedside log records bed, date, times and restarts; the run chart holds no names; charts are read by ward staff with routine access.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: families with limited English, low health literacy or who live far from the hospital may understand less or return elsewhere; the criteria card is translated into the two most common languages and the 7-day call uses interpreters.
response.effectiveness: Success is a sustained shift in time on high flow for infants aged 8 weeks or older without breaching the safety stopping rule.

response.title: Direct-cessation weaning of high-flow nasal cannula for infants with bronchiolitis: a ward quality improvement project
response.abstract: Problem: infants with bronchiolitis spent a median of 52 hours on high flow on a general pediatric ward, with weaning varying by attending. Intervention: a direct-cessation protocol for infants aged 8 weeks or older, tested in three PDSA cycles. Measures: weekly median time on high flow, with re-escalation, PICU transfer and 7-day readmission as balancing measures. Results will be reported after the season.
response.introduction: Direct cessation shortened time on high flow in a trial and a ward report, but the evidence for infants younger than 8 weeks conflicts, and night delivery of weaning checks is unreliable.
response.methods: Model for Improvement with the previous season as baseline and three cycles from November 2026 to March 2027. Run chart rules and a safety stopping rule were fixed in advance; infants under 8 weeks continued stepwise weaning and were followed descriptively. The project was screened as quality improvement.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present the run chart, the balancing measures, night adherence and the descriptive results for infants under 8 weeks.
response.discussion: The discussion will weigh any shift in time on high flow against the safety measures and state what the ward keeps; it will not claim safety for infants under 8 weeks.
response.limitations: Single ward, one season, historical baseline, and small numbers for safety outcomes.
response.conclusion: To be written after the season; limited to infants aged 8 weeks or older on this ward.
response.summary: SQUIRE-structured draft with results left empty until the season ends.
